..(Saturday night through Thursday)
Issued at 500 AM EDT FRI AUG 7 2026

The latest model data indicate that the pattern aloft mostly  
remains the same through the period with a broad ridge parked over
the bulk of the southwestern half of the nation well into next 
week. They also keep Kentucky on the southwest fringe of a large 
trough over all of northeast Canada yielding persistent northwest 
mid-level flow with periodic impulses passing by mainly north of 
the JKL forecast area. These should be close enough, though, to 
keep shower and thunderstorm chances in the forecast each day with
diurnal trends still dominant. Excessive rains will probably be 
isolated at best and due mainly to very site specific training. 

The previous long term discussion follows:

Scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms are still expected 
across Eastern Kentucky on Saturday, when broad mid/upper level 
troughing will remain in place over the Greater Ohio River Valley. A 
shortwave disturbance is still progged to propagate around the base 
of that trough during the initial stages of the forecast period, 
although it is notably quicker and less amplified than it was in 
previous model runs. The effects of those changes are twofold. 
First, there will probably be ongoing isolated to scattered 
convection when the period opens on Saturday morning. This 
introduces the potential for leftover cloud debris to decrease the 
magnitude of diurnal warming/destabilization, which, in turn, could 
limit the intensity of any activity that tries to develop later that 
afternoon/evening. Saturday morning has entered the temporal range 
of the 12z CAM runs, and many of those higher-resolution, convection-
allowing models support the idea that the PM convection will be 
weaker. A few models still try and develop afternoon/evening 
activity in SE KY, which is notably where the blended baseline 
guidance resolves the highest PoPs (55-75%). However, the convective 
parameter spacing appears marginal at best, with poor CAPE/shear 
balance and poor lapse rates. This is the second effect of the less-
amplified shortwave; storms are less likely to get organized and 
sustain themselves for longer periods of time. Severe storms appear 
unlikely on Saturday if these changes persist into future model 
runs.  

Model soundings do resolve between 1.7 and 1.9 inches of 
precipitable water in the atmospheric column over the forecast area 
on Saturday afternoon, along with freezing levels around 15kft and 
cloud-layer winds below 10 knots. If sufficient destabilization is 
realized and additional showers/storms develop across Eastern 
Kentucky on Saturday afternoon/evening, they will likely be 
efficient rainmakers and slow movers. Given the potential for 
localized pockets of already-wet soils from the activity described 
in the short term forecast period, Saturday's rainfall could once 
again prove excessive. The related flash flood risk is shrouded in 
the uncertainty though. The residual impacts of any AM activity 
and the evolution of the parent shortwave will determine whether or 
not such a risk actually materializes. WPC has maintained a broad-
brushed Marginal (Level 1/4) Excessive Rainfall Outlook for the 
entire JKL CWA on Saturday, but widespread flash flooding is not 
currently anticipated. Isolated instances cannot be ruled out in any 
locales that experience particularly persistent downpours or 
multiple rounds of torrential rainfall, as is typical during late 
summer in Eastern Kentucky. Interests in flood-prone places are 
encouraged to remain weather aware on Saturday, just in case. 

Another change in this morning's forecast guidance suite is the 
potential for yet another round of summertime showers/storms in 
Eastern Kentucky on Sunday. Both the GFS and the ECMWF had a QPF 
signal across portions of the CWA on Sunday afternoon in this 
morning's 12z data. It is intriguing that both deterministic models 
and their respective ensemble counterparts still resolve midlevel 
height rises in this same time frame. The troughing responsible for 
the early-weekend activity is progged to lift further to the 
northeast throughout the day on Sunday while ridging strengthens 
over the south-central CONUS. Those synoptic shifts place eastern KY 
within a regime of quasi-zonal flow aloft early next week. The 
related subsidence and midlevel dry air advection would reprieve our 
area from the recent repetitive marginal excessive rainfall risks. 
Thus, any convective activity that does occur in the Sunday-Monday 
time frame will likely be of the garden variety (sub-severe). It is 
plausible for future NBM baseline data to introduce isolated to 
scattered type PoPs to Sunday's forecast grids, so that will be a 
period to monitor for future adjustments. 

The attention then turns towards a series of ridge-riding shortwave 
impulses approaching the forecast area between Tuesday and Thursday.
